text: Once a table exists, you don't have to drop and recreate it just to change its shape. ALTER TABLE lets you add, modify, or remove columns on a table that may already have real rows sitting in it.

Alter table dbo dot LessonDemo, add Notes nvarchar 200 null. The new column appears on every existing row with a null value, unless you give it a default. Adding a nullable column is almost always safe, since SQL Server doesn't need to invent a value for rows that already exist.

Alter table dbo dot LessonDemo, alter column Label nvarchar 100 not null. This widens Label from fifty characters to a hundred. Growing a column is usually safe — it's shrinking one, or changing its type entirely, where the real caveat kicks in.

This fails if any existing Label value is longer than ten characters — SQL Server won't silently truncate your data just to make the alter succeed. Alter column always checks the data that's already there. If even one existing row can't fit the new type, the entire statement is rejected and nothing changes.

Alter table dbo dot LessonDemo, drop column Notes. This permanently removes the column and every value stored in it, for every row — there's no undo short of restoring a backup. It can also fail if a default constraint, check constraint, or index still references that column.
Next lesson: DROP TABLE, for removing a table entirely, plus the safe modern way to do it without an error if it's already gone.
